data: Make or Break?: The Literary Canon

This course explores how literary canons are formed by a multitude of different forces such as nation, culture, language, and economics. Beginning with a case study on the “western” or “English” canon in the form of one of the most canonical female writers of all time, this course teaches students how, why, and when certain “great” works gain their importance or place in the canon. In doing so, students will learn how certain forces of inclusion and exclusion create so-called literary canons. This course also asks students to consider what it would mean to imagine canons (or their absence) differently: for example, what would a “global” literary canon look like? How would you structure a canon of women’s literature? Do we need canons at all? To begin to answer these questions, our reading will explore the idea of the canon and its relationship to adaptations, translations, intertextuality, and literary prizes through key writers and texts and a trio of literary events in 2025: the global celebrations of the 250th anniversary of Jane Austen; the Nobel in Africa symposium in Stellenbosch, South Africa (November 2025), featuring literary prize-winners J.M. Coetzee and Abdulrazak Gurnah; and, closer to home in south India, the 2025 International Booker Prize for Heart Lamp to Banu Mushtaq and Deepa Bhasthi
